newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan repatriates two China hijackers -official.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan repatriates two China hijackers -official.

text.p: Taiwan on Wednesday repatriated two Chinese mainlanders who hijacked jetliners to the island in the early 1990s, in what it called an act of good faith reciprocating Beijing's May handover of an air pirate from Taiwan.

"We have completed the repatriation this morning," Chang Shu-ti of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council said after the two hijackers, a man and a woman, were handed over to Red Cross officials from the nearby mainland province of Fujian.

Han Fengying and Huang Shugang, who served out prison sentences for air piracy in Taiwan, could face trial in the communist mainland on similar charges, which can carry the death penalty. Beijing has not indicated whether they would be tried.

Han Fengying's son, whom she brought when she and her husband hijacked a jet from the mainland in 1993, was not handed over but remained in foster care in Taiwan, where Han's husband has not completed his prison sentence.
Taipei urged Beijing to adhere to the principles of humanity, security and convenience when handling the case.

The handover, conducted in a harbour in the Taiwan-held island of Quemoy, or Jinmen, just a few kilometres (miles) off the Fujian coast, was completed despite the lack of a repatriation pact between Taipei and Beijing, which have been arch rivals since a 1949 civil war split.

The first hijacker repatriation across the tense Taiwan strait was in May, when Beijing handed over Liu Shan-chung, a jobless journalist who hijacked a jetliner to the Fujian port of Xiamen in March, alleging he faced persecution in Taiwan.
Taipei said it welcomed Beijing's return of Liu, but urged the sides to resume their long-stalled talks "as soon as possible".

"We have noticed an act of good faith by the mainland side," the council said in a statement. "We hope both sides can continue to work together and crack down on crime to rectify the disorders across the Taiwan striat and maintain social stability," it said.
Including Han and Huang, Taiwan currently holds 16 mainlanders who hijacked 12 mainland planes to Taiwan in 1993-1994 before China tightened airport security.

Taiwan itself helped curb the tide of hijackings from the mainland by putting air pirates on trial and imprisoning them, a major shift from earlier decades when hijackers were hailed as anti-communist freedom fighters.
Beijing also has shifted policy, returning Taiwan hijacker Liu Shan-chung rather than letting him stay on and giving him a job, as it did with an earlier Taiwan air pirate.
Taiwan and China, which have no formal links since the 1949 split, reached consensus on hijacker repatriation in 1995 but did not sign the accord due to subsequent political friction.
Beijing froze bilateral negotiations 24 months ago to protest a landmark private visit to the United States by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui in mid-1995.
Beijing has consistently declined Taipei's call to resume semi-official talks, saying no dialogue would be possible until Taiwan agreed to stop engaging in what China called "splittist" activities.
